nameStory: The 'forked three-awn' gets its name from its most striking feature - each seed comes topped with three long, thin bristles called awns that split apart like the tines of a fork. The scientific name basiramea means 'branching from the base,' describing how this grass sends up multiple stems from its root system.
description: Forked three-awn grass is a native annual grass that forms small, wispy clumps in sandy or disturbed areas. It grows 1-2 feet tall with thin, delicate stems that branch from the base. The grass produces inconspicuous flowers that develop into distinctive seeds, each crowned with three spreading bristles that give the plant its memorable name.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Each seed has three long, thin bristles (awns) that fork outward like tiny pitchforks - run your finger gently along them and feel how they catch and pull

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Multiple thin, wiry stems branch from the base creating small, open clumps rather than dense mats

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, thread-like leaves that feel rough to the touch and curl slightly when dry

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, unremarkable flowers arranged in loose, open clusters that sway easily in the breeze

habitat: Look for forked three-awn grass in sandy, well-drained soils in open areas like disturbed roadsides, old fields, and woodland edges. It thrives in poor, dry soils where other grasses struggle. In New England, it's quite rare and most likely found in southern areas with sandier conditions.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small tufts of thin, bright green leaves sprouting from sandy soil.
seasonality.summer: Stems elongate and produce their small flowers, which are easy to overlook among the wispy foliage.
seasonality.fall: Seeds develop their characteristic three-pronged awns, making this the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist, showing the distinctive branching pattern and scattered three-awned seeds.

funFact: The three-pronged seeds are like tiny grappling hooks - they grab onto fur, feathers, and clothing so effectively that each awn can twist and drill the seed into the ground when it gets wet, essentially planting itself!
confusionNotes: Other three-awn grasses in New England can look very similar, but pay attention to the branching pattern - forked three-awn branches mainly from the base rather than higher up on the stem. The three awns on each seed are the definitive feature that separates all three-awn grasses from other native grasses.
contextualKnowledge: This is one of New England's rarest grasses with only 2 recorded observations in the region, making any sighting quite special. Three-awn grasses as a group are much more common and diverse in the American Southwest and Great Plains.
compareHints: Among New England's three-awn grasses, forked three-awn is distinguished by its branching pattern from the base rather than higher up the stem like fork-tip three-awn. It's smaller and more delicate than arrowfeather threeawn, and lacks the coastal habitat preference of seaside threeawn.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the three-awn grasses in New England, Slim-spike has the most delicate, narrow flower spikes - much thinner than the more robust spikes of Arrowfeather Threeawn or the branched clusters of Fork-tip Three-awn.

Arrowfeather threeawn is typically taller and more robust than most of its relatives like fork-tip three-awn, and its seed bristles are usually longer and more feathery than the shorter, stiffer bristles of oldfield three-awn.
Among its three-awn relatives in New England, Oldfield Three-awn is the most delicate and branched, with the most open, airy seed heads.
Among New England's three-awn grasses, fork-tip three-awn is unique for its distinctly forked branching pattern and smaller size.
Seaside Threeawn is distinguished from other New England threeawns primarily by its coastal habitat - it's the only species in the genus that grows directly in beach sand and tolerates salt spray.
